---
title: "Making Content via the Repository Interface"
---

I recommend you work on understanding the [web interface](web-interface.qmd) before reading this page. In fact, it is possible to work with PrairieLearn _only_ via the web interface. However, consider the following questions:

- Will you create hundreds of questions in PrairieLearn?
- Would you like some of your questions to be significantly more complex than the [example question](web-interface.qmd#question) you made via the web interface?
- Would you like to be able to leverage agentic AI in your question development? That is, are you interested in using prompts like the (abbreviated) examples below:
    - **Bulk Generation**: Generate 10 questions similar to Lecture 7 examples and add them to a new assessment.
    - **Format Conversion**: Convert these 5 multiple-choice questions into short-answer questions.
    - **Metadata & Tagging**: Find all questions discussing topic X and append tag Y to their tag lists.
    - **Parameter Randomization**: For cleaner math, modify Q1–Q5 to generate single-digit integer values instead of real numbers.
    - **Scope Verification**: Verify that all questions in this assessment use only concepts covered in Lectures 1 through 8.
    - **Bug & Edge-Case Audit**: Check all questions in this assessment to ensure random parameters never cause zero-division errors.
    - **Randomness Audit**: Generate 1000 variants of this question using its current randomization parameters, and ensure all edge cases are handled correctly.
    - **Difficulty & Weighting**: Identify difficulty outliers in this assessment and critique the assigned point values.
    - **Dynamic Explanations**: Write step-by-step student feedback (consistent with randomized variables) for wrong answers in this question.

If you answered "yes" to any of the above, I strongly recommend you learn how to work directly with your PrairieLearn GitHub repository ("repo"), as described on this page.

::: {.callout-tip}
I know that for some people, the idea of working with a GitHub repository feels intimidating, like it's just for experienced programmers and one wrong move might break something. I'll offer two points of reassurance!

First, the handful of GitHub actions you'll actually use here are simple to learn, and nothing is fragile or permanent. Any mistakes are easy to undo.

Second, using the tools on this page is not the same as coding, and with AI, no coding is required for PrairieLearn at all. Please also know that as the faculty advisor to the ETF, I'm happy to help you get set up. I want to help remove roadblocks so you can achieve your goals. Feel free to reach out anytime at etf-advisor@umich.edu.
:::

## Tools to Install

First, you'll need to install a few things, just as a one-time setup.

### Git

For our purposes, think of Git as a small set of programs that enable you to interact with GitHub.com outside of a web browser. Installation depends on whether your computer is running Windows or macOS.

#### Windows Users

Go to the [git-scm.com Windows page](https://git-scm.com/install/windows) and download the "x64 version of Git for Windows". I recommend you choose the first option, labeled "x64 version of Git for Windows", unless you know you need something else. Download the file and run it to install Git.

#### macOS Users

There are brief instructions at [git-scm.com macOS page](https://git-scm.com/install/mac) that some may find helpful, but for most users, I recommend you follow the more detailed version below instead.

1. Press <kbd>Cmd</kbd>+<kbd>Space</kbd>, type "Terminal", and press <kbd>Enter</kbd>. This opens a special program called the _terminal_, with which we can give special instructions to your computer. If you've never used the terminal before, that's ok! The one-time instructions below walk you through it step by step.
2. In the terminal, type or paste the following command:

    ```bash
    xcode-select --install
    ```
    - Note that there is a single dash between "xcode" and "select", a space after "select", and a double dash before "install".
3. Press <kbd>Enter</kbd> so that the command above is run.
4. A window will pop up, asking you about installing "command line developer tools" (including Git). Choose to install the tools, and agree to the license.

   ::: {.callout-tip}
   If instead you see a message saying the command line tools are already installed, then you can skip the remaining steps.
   :::

5. Installation runs in the background and may take a few minutes. You can leave the window as-is until it finishes.
6. When the installation is complete, you can verify that the installation worked by entering the following command in the terminal and hitting <kbd>Enter</kbd>:

    ```bash
    git --version
    ```

    You should see a version number printed in the terminal, which indicates that Git is installed and working correctly.
7. When the installation is complete, you can close the window.

### Python

Python is a programming language. As I promised before, you won't have to write any code to develop PrairieLearn questions. Your computer will need Python installed, though. To do this, go to the [Python downloads page](https://www.python.org/downloads/) and download the latest version of Python for your operating system. Run the installer and follow the prompts to install Python; ***on Windows***, be sure to check the box that says "Add Python to PATH" before installing.

### An Integrated Development Environment and AI Agent

Next, you will need an integrated development environment (IDE). An IDE is a special program that makes it easier to work with code. We'll use an AI agent inside of an IDE to work with your PrairieLearn repo on your behalf.

If you already have experience with IDEs and AI agent integration, then stick with what you know. Otherwise, I recommend using VS Code with Claude Code.

#### Installing VS Code

Go to the [VS Code downloads page](https://code.visualstudio.com/) and download the installer for your operating system (Windows or macOS). Run the installer and accept the defaults.

#### Setting Up Claude Code

Claude Code is an AI extension for VS Code. Once installed, it can read, write, and edit files in your repo directly, following your instructions.

If you want AI assistance with more than minimal usage, you'll need a subscription. There are two ways U-M faculty members might choose to pursue this:

- **Personal subscription**: Follow the setup instructions in the [Claude Code documentation for VS Code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/vs-code). This walks you through installing the extension and signing in with a Claude.ai account. Anecdotally, at time of writing, I've found the $20/month subscription to be sufficient and highly worthwhile for PrairieLearn development.
- **U-M GPT Toolkit**: Use Claude Code through the [U-M GPT Toolkit](https://its.umich.edu/computing/ai/claude-code-gpt-toolkit), with usage-based pricing billed through the university rather than a personal subscription. See the link for setup details.

::: {.callout-tip}
You may be aware that U-M also provides free access to several AI models (including Claude) through a [chat-only interface](https://umgpt.umich.edu/). That's a fine way to get a feel for AI-assisted question writing at no cost, but note that it can't directly edit files in your repo the way an IDE-integrated AI agent can. So it won't support the more advanced, hands-off workflows described earlier on this page (bulk generation, scope verification, and similar), where the AI is directly reading and editing your repo's files rather than you copying content back and forth by hand.
:::

## Cloning Your Repo

As briefly mentioned above, your PrairieLearn course (including questions and assessments) is stored in the GitHub repo that you gained access to when your course was created. This basically means that your course is stored "in the cloud". We need to get a local copy of it; this is called "cloning" the repo.

1. Open VS Code.
2. Open the Command Palette (<kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>P</kbd> on Windows, <kbd>Cmd</kbd>+<kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>P</kbd> on Mac), type "Git: Clone", and press <kbd>Enter</kbd>.
3. Choose "Clone from GitHub". The first time you do this, VS Code will open your browser and ask you to sign in to GitHub.com and authorize VS Code. Approve this.
4. Back in VS Code, a list of your GitHub repositories will appear (or you can search for it by name). Select your PrairieLearn course's repository.

   ::: {.callout-tip}
   If you don't see your PrairieLearn course's repository in the list, you may not have accepted the invitation email sent when your PrairieLearn course was created (see [Getting Access](index.qmd#access)). Email [support@prairielearn.com](mailto:support@prairielearn.com) to request a new invitation.
   :::

5. Choose a folder on your computer where you'd like to keep your PrairieLearn files.
6. Choose to open the repository when prompted.

Your course files are now on your computer, and open in VS Code.

::: {.callout-tip}
If you prefer the terminal, open a terminal in VS Code and run this command, replacing the example URL with your own repository's URL (found by clicking the green "Code" button on your repository's page on GitHub.com, under the "HTTPS" tab):

```bash
git clone https://github.com/YOUR-ORGANIZATION/YOUR-REPOSITORY.git
```
:::

## Opening and Exploring Your Repo

Open your Repo in your IDE. For example, if you're using VS Code, start it, click on "File" in the top menu, then "Open Folder". Navigate to the folder where you cloned your repo and open it. You should see a list of files and folders in the left-hand panel.

Explore the folder structure a bit, and open the files you see. You should recognize some of the files you saw in the web interface. For example, in the `questions` folder, there should be a subfolder for each question you created, and inside each of those subfolders are the files that define the question: info.json, question.html, and server.py. Similarly, note the `assessments` folder contents.

Now, you can edit these files directly in your IDE, and also ask AI to do it for you.

## Keeping Everything in Sync

We now have three copies of your course:

1. The local code on your computer
2. The remote code in your GitHub repo
3. The code in the PrairieLearn web interface

This I promise you: if you don't keep these copies in sync, it will tear up your heart and your happiness will go bye bye bye. The syncing steps depend on whether you edit your local code or via the web interface, as described in the subsections below.

::: {.callout-warning}
**Avoid syncing conflicts:** To keep things simple, don't edit your content both locally and on the web interface between syncs. Rather, pick one place to work at a time and sync before switching.
:::

### If You Edit Your Local Code

```{mermaid}
%%{init: {'themeVariables': {'edgeLabelBackground': '#FFFFFF', 'primaryTextColor': '#00274C'}}}%%
flowchart LR
    A["💻 ✏️ Edit<br><b>Local Code</b><br>(your computer)"] -->|push| B["☁️<br><b>Remote Repo</b><br>(GitHub.com)"]
    B -->|sync| C["🌐<br><b>Web Interface</b><br>(PrairieLearn)"]

    classDef umNode fill:#00274C,stroke:#FFCB05,stroke-width:3px,color:#FFFFFF
    class A,B,C umNode
    linkStyle default stroke:#00274C,stroke-width:3px
```

When you edit files in your local code (e.g., with VS Code), you first need to _push_ those changes back to the GitHub.com repo so that PrairieLearn can see them. The easiest way to do this is through VS Code's built-in Source Control panel:

1. Click the Source Control icon in the left-hand activity bar (it looks like three connected dots and is labeled "Source Control" when you hover over it; it often shows a number badge for changed files).
2. You'll see a list of your changed files. Hover over "Changes" and click the "+" icon to stage all of them (or stage individual files the same way).
3. Type a short message describing what you changed (e.g., "Added new question about linear equations") in the message box at the top.
4. Click the blue "Commit" button, then click "Sync Changes" (or "Push") to send your changes to GitHub.com.

If you prefer the terminal, open a terminal in VS Code (Terminal menu, "New Terminal") and run these three commands in your repo folder, in order:

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Describe your changes here"
git push
```

Next, we need to tell the PL web interface to _sync_ the course so that it sees the changes we just pushed. Click the "Sync" tab on the left side, and then the blue "Pull from remote git repository" button. When the process completes successfully, your course has been updated! You can verify this by looking at the changed items (e.g., questions, assessments) in the web interface.

### If You Edit Via the Web Interface

```{mermaid}
%%{init: {'themeVariables': {'edgeLabelBackground': '#FFFFFF', 'primaryTextColor': '#00274C'}}}%%
flowchart LR
    C["🌐 ✏️ Edit<br><b>Web Interface</b><br>(PrairieLearn)"] -->|auto-<br>sync| B["☁️<br><b>Remote Repo</b><br>(GitHub.com)"]
    B -->|pull| A["💻<br><b>Local Code</b><br>(your computer)"]

    classDef umNode fill:#00274C,stroke:#FFCB05,stroke-width:3px,color:#FFFFFF
    class A,B,C umNode
    linkStyle default stroke:#00274C,stroke-width:3px
```

Similarly, if you make changes to your PrairieLearn course via the web interface, we need to get those changes to your local code. The first step of this happens automatically: when you make changes in the web interface, those changes are _automatically synced_ to your GitHub.com repo. Thus, all that remains is to pull those changes to your local repo.

In VS Code, click the Source Control icon in the left-hand activity bar and click the "..." (More Actions) menu at the top, then choose "Pull" (or simply click the sync/refresh icon in the bottom status bar if you see one). Your local files will be updated to match what's on GitHub.com.

If you prefer the terminal, open a terminal in VS Code and run this command in your repo folder:

```bash
git pull
```

## Resources for your Repo

I recommend you download these [useful PrairieLearn files](files/pl_for_UM.zip) and copy them into the root of your PrairieLearn repo. That is, after copying, your repo should have folders called `serverFilesCourse` and `tools` at the root (not inside some sub-folder), and your questions folder should have a templates folder inside of it. The templates folder contains several example questions. These templates show you or an AI agent what syntax is needed to create various types of content. You may find it useful to refer to them in any prompts for creating questions.

## Next Steps

For further examples of question generation, you may find this [Engineering Education Innovation day presentation](https://drive.google.com/drive/u/0/folders/15-LHxlP8fdFuVQwbnK4clguFPSfcxAfV) by Laura Alford and Steven Bogaerts to be useful. It includes illustration of question generation through both the [web interface](web-interface.qmd) and the [repository interface](github-repo.qmd).
